source.title: Forecasting Frontier Language Model Agent Capabilities
source.authors: Govind Pimpale; Axel Højmark; Jérémy Scheurer; Marius Hobbhahn

record.tranche_reason: The study tests downstream benchmark predictability using expanding-window backtesting, but uses linear and sigmoidal forecasting relationships rather than testing held-out pretraining loss power laws.
record.gate_note: The study cites prior scaling-law results and uses Hoffmann scaling laws to normalize training FLOP estimates, but does not test those loss laws or compute-optimal allocations. Its agent benchmark scores and forecasts are not recorded as separate evidence rows: the forecasts are projections, not observed future outcomes, and the individual scores are inputs to its forecasting analyses. The recorded results are its reported backtesting RMSEs.
record.test_reason: The study fits sigmoids of benchmark score on scaled training log-FLOP and backtests them on held-out later models (R3, R5, R7, R9). That is a direct test of whether downstream performance is predictable from scale (V6). The other rows use release date or capability metrics (PC-1, Elo) as predictors, which are neither scale nor pretraining loss. Hoffmann laws are only assumed, to normalise FLOP.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Release Date→PC-1→Benchmark backtests best (RMSE 0.082), and Release Date→Elo→Benchmark is second (0.095); release date outperforms log-FLOP as an input. The latter path is used to forecast SWE-Bench Verified at 54% (low elicitation) and 87% (high elicitation) by January 2026; the introduction says 55%/85%, which is inconsistent with the abstract. The authors note the forecasts may be conservative because inference-time scaling is not modelled.
record.recipe_differences: The study forecasts downstream benchmark scores with linear intermediate-metric fits and sigmoid score fits; it does not fit held-out loss power laws or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Backtested errors vary by input variable and intermediate metric; Release Date → PC-1 performs best, while Release Date → Elo is second-best. The high- and low-elicitation forecasts also use different data inclusion rules and scaffolds.

fits_no_version.finding: Benchmark scores are predicted from release date (directly, or via Elo/PC-1) and from cross-benchmark capability metrics, with backtest RMSEs of 0.068–0.146. Release-date paths beat log-FLOP paths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream benchmark scores of frontier LMs are predictable from release date or from latent capability metrics, at least as well as from training compute.

record.problems: The authors note a small number of frontier models and short backtesting windows, in some cases as brief as two months, limiting evidence about longer-term forecasting. Backtesting results are aggregated and have no uncertainty estimates reported alongside the RMSEs.
record.rows_left_out: No backtesting rows omitted. Individual agent benchmark scores and projected future scores in Table 3, Figure 1, and Figure 5 were not extracted as separate rows because the individual scores are data used by the forecasting analysis and the future values are projections rather than observed prediction outcomes.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not measured. Hoffmann laws are only assumed, to compute scaled FLOP.
Extrapolation of loss power laws to larger runs.
Effects of architecture shape on loss.
Prediction from pretraining loss. Prediction of agent benchmarks (SWE-Bench, Cybench, RE-Bench) from scale: the agent forecasts use release date only and are not backtested.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting choices.

missing.what: Linear fits of PC-1 and Elo on scaled log-FLOP for frontier models, R² ≥ 0.91 (Figure 3). This also includes the date-based fits, which are not V6.
Per-benchmark and per-split backtest RMSEs for log-FLOP, as opposed to the aggregates only

record.verdict_notes: The FLOP measure is 'scaled' compute, normalised with Hoffmann loss laws, so it assumes V3/V1 rather than testing them. Fits are sigmoids on log-FLOP, not power laws. There is no naive baseline, so the RMSEs cannot be graded against chance; states are therefore partial. The frontier sample is small and some backtest windows are two months long. The agent-benchmark forecasts are projections, not tests.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of loss power laws from small runs to much larger runs.
The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation trend and its growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests predictability of downstream benchmark scores, not whether performance improves with held-out pretraining loss specifically.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup, fit choices, or curve bending.

relationships.condition: Backtested prediction of OpenLLM v2 benchmark scores from scaled log-FLOP (38 models, short windows)
relationships.reason: Out-of-sample RMSE is about 0.10–0.20 (R3, R5, R7, R9). Accuracy depends on the pathway (0.197 via Elo) and is worse than release-date or capability-metric predictors.
relationships.display_finding: Out-of-sample RMSE was about 0.10–0.20, including 0.197 through Elo, and exceeded errors from release-date or capability predictors.

relation.reason: The study reports its own held-out benchmark prediction errors for scaled log-FLOP pathways, directly bearing on V6.

tranche.reason: Sigmoid benchmark-score fits and expanding-window backtests test downstream predictability from scaled training compute using a different method and measure from pretraining-loss scaling.

source_check.notes: No no-skill baseline is reported, so absolute RMSE alone does not establish weak predictability; the scope limitation rests on pathway comparisons and short validation windows. Appendix D contains example scaffold prompts, which are excluded from instruction detection.

statements.correction: Section 3: backtests on six Open LLM Leaderboard v2 benchmarks. Section 4.2: agent forecasts use Release Date→Elo→Benchmark. No Cybench or RE-Bench training-scale backtest is reported.
statements.problem: The distinction between leaderboard backtests and agent forecasts is correct, but the paper does not explicitly state that its agent forecasts are not backtested; this follows from the reported methods and results.
